lessons.title: Proof of Work vs Proof of Stake
lessons.description: Understand the two most important consensus mechanisms in crypto — and why Ethereum switched.

content.text: How Do Blockchains Agree?

A blockchain has thousands of computers around the world — none of which trust each other. To add a new block of transactions, they all need to agree on what happened. The rules they use to reach that agreement is called a **consensus mechanism**. The two dominant approaches are Proof of Work (PoW) and Proof of Stake (PoS).
⛏️ Proof of Work (PoW)

In PoW, computers called **miners** race to solve a complex mathematical puzzle. The first to solve it earns the right to add the next block and receives a reward in cryptocurrency. Bitcoin still uses PoW today.

**Key properties:**
- Requires enormous computing power (and electricity)
- The difficulty adjusts so a block is found roughly every 10 minutes
- An attacker would need 51% of all mining power to cheat
🪙 Proof of Stake (PoS)

In PoS, participants called **validators** lock up ("stake") their own cryptocurrency as collateral. The network randomly selects a validator to add the next block — the more you stake, the higher your chance. Ethereum switched to PoS in September 2022 in an event called **The Merge**.

**Key properties:**
- Uses ~99.95% less energy than PoW
- Validators risk losing their staked coins if they cheat ("slashing")
- Lower barrier to entry than mining hardware

lessons.title: What is a Blockchain?
lessons.description: Discover how blockchains work, why they can't be changed, and who maintains them.

content.text: The World's Most Tamper-Proof Ledger

A **blockchain** is a distributed ledger — a shared record of transactions that is copied across thousands of computers worldwide. Unlike a bank database controlled by one company, no single person owns or controls a public blockchain. Every participant has a full copy of the entire history.
🧱 Blocks, Chains, and Hashes

Transactions are grouped into **blocks**. Each block contains:
- A batch of transactions
- A timestamp
- A **hash** (a unique fingerprint of its own data)
- The hash of the **previous** block

This chaining of hashes is what makes blockchains immutable. If you change one block, its hash changes — breaking the link to every block after it. The network immediately detects the fraud.
🌐 Decentralization & Nodes

A **node** is any computer running the blockchain software. There are thousands of nodes, each holding a complete copy of the ledger. To add a fraudulent transaction, you'd have to rewrite the history on the majority of all nodes simultaneously — practically impossible.

lessons.title: Wallets, Keys & Addresses
lessons.description: Learn how crypto wallets, private keys, and public addresses keep your funds secure.

content.text: Your Keys, Your Crypto

A common misconception is that a crypto wallet stores coins. It doesn't. Your coins live on the blockchain. A wallet stores your **private keys** — the secret codes that prove you own those coins and authorize you to send them.
🔑 Private Keys, Public Keys & Addresses

**Private key** — A secret code (like a password) that must never be shared. Anyone with your private key controls your crypto.

**Public key / Address** — Derived from your private key, this is safe to share. It's like your bank account number — people use it to send you crypto.

**Seed phrase** — A set of 12 or 24 random words that can regenerate your private key. Back this up offline and guard it like cash.
🔥 Hot Wallets vs ❄️ Cold Wallets

**Hot wallet** — Connected to the internet (e.g. MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet). Convenient for frequent use but more vulnerable to hacks.

**Cold wallet** — Stored offline (e.g. Ledger, Trezor hardware devices). Much safer for large amounts you don't need to access daily.

**Non-custodial** — You hold your own keys. **Custodial** — An exchange holds your keys (e.g. leaving coins on Coinbase).

lessons.title: Transactions & Gas Fees
lessons.description: Learn how crypto transactions work, what gas fees are, and why they change.

content.text: Sending Crypto — What Actually Happens?

When you send cryptocurrency, you're broadcasting a signed message to the network saying: "I authorize moving X coins from my address to yours." This message goes into a waiting area called the **mempool** until a miner or validator picks it up and includes it in the next block.
⛽ What Are Gas Fees?

On Ethereum, every transaction requires **gas** — a unit measuring computational effort. You pay a **gas fee** in ETH to compensate validators for processing your transaction.

- **Gas price** — how much you're willing to pay per unit of gas (in Gwei)
- **Gas limit** — the maximum gas your transaction can consume
- **Total fee** = Gas used × Gas price

When the network is busy, fees spike because users compete to get their transactions included first.
✅ Confirmations & Finality

Once included in a block, your transaction has **1 confirmation**. Each subsequent block adds another. Bitcoin typically needs **6 confirmations** (~60 minutes) to be considered final. Faster networks like Solana achieve finality in under a second with much lower fees.

lessons.title: Smart Contracts & DeFi
lessons.description: Explore self-executing code on the blockchain and how it powers decentralized finance.

content.text: Code That Executes Itself

A **smart contract** is a program stored on the blockchain that automatically executes when predefined conditions are met — no bank, lawyer, or middleman required. Think of it as a vending machine: insert the right input, get the predetermined output every time.
🏦 What is DeFi?

**DeFi (Decentralized Finance)** uses smart contracts to recreate financial services — lending, borrowing, trading, earning interest — without banks or brokers. Anyone with a wallet can access DeFi protocols 24/7 from anywhere in the world.

**Key DeFi concepts:**
- **DEX** — A decentralized exchange where users trade directly via smart contracts
- **Liquidity pool** — Funds deposited by users that enable trading on a DEX
- **Yield farming** — Earning rewards by providing liquidity to DeFi protocols
⚠️ Smart Contract Risks

Smart contracts are only as good as the code they're written in. Bugs or vulnerabilities can be exploited by hackers — and because they're immutable, a bad contract can't simply be patched. Billions of dollars have been lost to smart contract exploits. Always use audited protocols.
